title: GEOGRAPHICAL STORIES #001 · São Miguel: Island of Fire and Water
description: R2 Director’s Cut · five minutes, 45 shots, expanded documentary script, geographic markers, DEM hillshade, phased illustrations, chapter narration and original sound design.
author: OpenMotion Studio

documentary.narration: Why do volcanic cliffs rise from the Atlantic
while freshwater fills enormous craters

documentary.narration: and steam rises from the ground?
On São Miguel, even lunch has a geological story.

bucketList.imageAuthor: José Luís Ávila Silveira / Pedro Noronha e Costa

documentary.narration: This is the island of fire and water.
Far from continental shores, nine volcanic islands form the Azores, an autonomous region of Portugal.
The archipelago occupies a complex region where three major tectonic plates meet.
North American, Eurasian and African plates move relative to each other.
Extension and mantle melting help explain the region's widespread volcanism.
São Miguel lies in the eastern group, stretching roughly sixty-two kilometres.
Its coastline reveals the accumulated work of volcanic eruptions.
The island's oldest exposed rocks record millions of years of volcanic activity.
Magma reached the seabed repeatedly, building volcanic mountains until some rose above the waves.
Fluid lava builds flows, while explosive eruptions scatter ash and pumice across surrounding land.
Waves erode the volcanic coast, exposing layers left behind by successive eruptions.
Sete Cidades, Fogo and Furnas are the three active central volcanoes, separated by fissure systems.
Older volcanic centres in the east complete the island's mountainous geography.
At the western end, the Sete Cidades volcano holds a caldera about five kilometres wide.
During major eruptions, magma is withdrawn from a reservoir, reducing support beneath the summit.
The overlying rock subsides. Rain and runoff accumulate in the depression over time.
Lagoa Azul and Lagoa Verde are connected sections of the lake on the caldera floor.
Water depth, light and biological conditions influence how the two sections appear.

bucketList.imageAuthor: José Luís Ávila Silveira / Pedro Noronha e Costa

documentary.narration: A village occupies the sheltered basin, framed by steep walls and agricultural land.
Further east lies Fogo, also called Água de Pau, another large volcanic centre.
Its lake occupies a high caldera where steep slopes funnel water toward the basin.

bucketList.imageAuthor: José Luís Ávila Silveira / Pedro Noronha e Costa

documentary.narration: In fifteen sixty-three, an explosive eruption reshaped the landscape during the early centuries of settlement.
Ash and pumice from explosive eruptions leave deposits that record previous volcanic events.
Clouds, rain and wind now work on the same slopes once formed by volcanic activity.
At Furnas, the volcanic system becomes visible through hot springs and steam vents.
Rainwater enters cracks in the rock. Heat from below warms water circulating underground.
Hot water and gases rise toward the surface through permeable rock and fractures.

bucketList.imageAuthor: José Luís Ávila Silveira / Pedro Noronha e Costa

documentary.narration: At the surface, mineral deposits and steaming streams reveal the transfer of underground heat.
Local cooks lower sealed pots into hot ground, using the natural heat to cook slowly.
The traditional stew is a direct connection between geology, local knowledge and everyday life.
The Atlantic supplies moist air. As air rises over mountains, it cools and condenses.
Frequent rainfall feeds streams and waterfalls, especially where water descends steep volcanic valleys.
Weathering of volcanic material, rainfall and vegetation help form the soils of São Miguel.
Pastures cover much of the agricultural landscape, with dairy farming important to the island.
Tea plantations take advantage of the mild oceanic climate and suitable growing conditions.
Along the southern coast, Ponta Delgada's harbour connects the island to the wider world.
Volcanic heat continues to influence this landscape.

bucketList.imageAuthor: José Luís Ávila Silveira / Pedro Noronha e Costa

documentary.narration: Rain and erosion continue to transform the volcanic terrain.
People have adapted to the opportunities and limits of the island's geography.
São Miguel's story is a reminder that geological landscapes are never finished.
Understanding our planet, one place at a time.
